title: Range of outcomes (Monte Carlo)
question: How wide could the price range be over the coming months, and how much do earnings days add to that uncertainty?

tables.title: AAPL: Range of outcomes after 12 months (random-walk model, not a forecast)

tables.title: Earnings days taken out of the normal-day sample

charts.title: Range of outcomes, 100 = today's price (random-walk model, not a forecast)

findings: Under a random-walk model (not a forecast), 90% of simulated outcomes after 12 months fall between 222 $ and 535 $; the middle half between 286 $ and 413 $. Today: 356 $.

In real markets very large moves (down and up) happen more often than in this model (fat tails); calm and stormy spells cluster; if conditions change, the past 3 years stop applying. This range is a model result.
Earnings days move ~2,1× as much as normal days (median absolute move 1,6 % vs 0,8 %; 12 releases in 3 years). 5,7 % of the 12-month uncertainty comes from these 4 days.

The model assumes no edge: the average outcome equals today’s price (356 $), yet the median is 343 $ — volatility pulls the typical path below the average. Probability of ending below today: 55,8 % (this is not an expected fall; even with zero edge the median sits below today).
In the model, probability of touching −20% at some close along the way: 43,7 % (annualised normal-day volatility 26,2 %).
notes: This is a range of outcomes under a random-walk model, not a forecast: geometric Brownian motion (a random walk in log prices) scaled to the stock’s last 3 years. It is not a buy/sell recommendation or a price target.
Data: daily adjusted closes over the last 3 years (2023-11-13 – 2026-11-13), log returns. Volatility (sigma) from normal days only: 1,65% a day.
Zero edge: the expected (arithmetic) return is set to zero — daily log drift = −sigma²/2. Past returns are not carried forward.
Simulation: 10,000 paths, daily steps, 21 trading days a month (252 days), fixed seed 20261112 (same input → same output). Monte Carlo standard error of the mean ≈ 0,27% of today’s price.

Earnings days: SEC 8-K “Item 2.02” dates; the reaction day is the first trading day on/after the filing (the next day when filed after the close). These days were taken out of the normal-day sample so they are not counted twice. Jump = reaction-day log return − mean normal-day return; the next results dates are projected from the past spacing (~91 days) and each draws, with replacement, from the stock’s own 12 jumps. Jumps are shifted so they add no expected return either.
Variance share = jumps × var(jump) / (jumps × var(jump) + days × sigma²). The reaction-day sample also contains that day’s normal noise, a small overlap (one day per release).

Fat tails: excess kurtosis of normal days is 10,2 (0 for a normal distribution). Real markets produce very large moves (down and up) more often than this model; read the 5% and 95% ends not as limits but as points the real outcome can lie beyond.

Volatility clustering: calm and stormy spells come in runs (lag-1 autocorrelation of squared returns 0,24). The model uses one constant sigma; the last 63 days ran at 22,3 % vs 26,2 % for 3-year normal days.
Regime changes and model risk: if the company, rates or the market change, the past 3 years do not represent the future. Brownian motion is a simplification; the answer depends on these assumptions.
The −20% touch probability uses daily closes (intraday lows are not counted). Holidays are ignored (weekdays = trading days).

Why −σ²/2? Itô’s lemma: if dS = μS dt + σS dW then d ln S = (μ − σ²/2) dt + σ dW. Keeping the expected return at zero needs a log drift of −σ²/2, which is why the median outcome sits slightly below today’s price. Analysis #29 (Brownian motion and Itô’s lemma) tests how well these assumptions hold for this stock.
